title: Child‐Directed Communication in Two Diverse Cultural Contexts
abstract: ABSTRACT There is significant variability across societies regarding the prevalence of infant‐directed speech (IDS) when adults are addressing infants and young children. For example, there are reports of significantly less IDS in some societies—including families on Tanna, Vanuatu—which is surprising given that IDS is widely assumed to be a prominent feature of human caregiving. However, the assumption of universality of IDS is largely based on findings from urban societies; therefore it is possible that IDS is only one of several caregiving behaviours that are produced during interactions with infants and young children. To have a better understanding of the range of qualitative differences in communicative behaviours across cultures, we examined 85 video‐recorded observations of caregivers and their 18–24‐month‐old children living on Tanna, Vanuatu and in Vancouver, Canada. Video observations were approximately 10 min long, collected between 2013 and 2018 and were semi‐structured such that we either provided a set of toys or did not provide toys. We determined the proportion of time caregivers spent engaging in both verbal and non‐verbal interactions with their children using four different interaction codes: infant‐directed speech (IDS), infant‐directed non‐verbal behaviour (IDB), infant‐directed communication (IDC; defined as simultaneous IDS and IDB) and Solo (no interaction or attentive non‐interference). Caregivers in Vancouver were more likely to use IDS across both types of observations (toys and no‐toys), whereas caregivers on Tanna used more IDB when toys were present and more IDC without toys (but IDC was marginally more common in Vancouver with toys). Solo behaviours were similarly likely across both societies. Our findings suggest that there are diverse ways of supporting language development through coordinated interactions beyond infant‐directed speech. Cross‐cultural studies will help elucidate the range and variability of IDS and IDC in human populations.
